name: A Bit Walkery
summary: All 1,940 chips are required. The main obstacle is opening the double-chip boundary around a continuously cloned walker corridor without being trapped by the released walkers. No winning replay or complete impossibility argument is established.
proofSteps: The source walker at (6,2) faces west on a cloner. A ball repeatedly crosses the connected red button at (23,3), filling the corridor from (2,2) to (6,2).

The surrounding chips initially contain the walkers. Removing the last chip from a boundary cell admits monsters into that cell; a state can appear alive until the next monster movement phase, when Chip may be killed before being able to leave.

A bounded opening search found a legal prefix that collects all 18 chips on the nine corridor-adjacent cells by tick 115 and has at least one surviving continuation. This rules out treating those cells as permanently inaccessible. It does not establish a complete solution.
limitations: No winning replay and no universal impossibility proof established. Data counts or unsuccessful play are not treated as impossibility.

experiments.result: Decoded both 1024-cell DAT planes and exact level metadata; initialized production MS runtime and rendered actual game sprites.
A deterministic collection attempt reached 20 chips remaining before time became limiting. The remaining cells were concentrated near the walker cloner. This was not a winning replay.

Used a fixed seed and stepping value to search movement choices around the cloner after inspecting its mechanism. A next-window survival check rejected apparently successful openings that were killed on the following monster phase. Clearing the full surrounding region and finishing the level remain unresolved.

The 116-input opening that clears the 18 critical adjacent chips also matches the native final state: alive at (1,2), tick 115, with 1914 of 1940 chips still required. Exact replay bytes were read and native stderr was empty. This is a partial route, not a win.
